# Chapter 17 — Role-Based Administration — Replacing OU-Based Delegation

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
How administrative delegation — the ability to scope helpdesk, IT, and
management authority to a subset of users — is reconstructed in Entra ID
using Administrative Units, OrgPath facet predicates, and PIM. Chapter 6
showed that AUs do not inherit; this chapter shows how OrgPath membership
rules eliminate the need for inheritance.
:::

## The Problem Chapter 6 Left Open

Chapter 6 established that Administrative Units are a real delegation
mechanism — but one with a critical structural gap. In Active Directory,
assigning a role at the `OU=West-Region` level automatically covered every
sub-OU beneath it. Entra ID AUs do not work that way. Each AU is
independent. A role assigned to the West Region AU does not flow to the
West Finance AU or the West IT AU. Every level requires its own explicit
role assignment.

This leaves administrators facing an apparent dilemma: either flatten the
delegation model to a handful of tenant-wide roles (which destroys
granularity), or maintain dozens of manual per-AU role assignments (which
creates drift and operational overhead that increases with organizational
complexity).

OrgPath resolves this dilemma by making AU membership rules deterministic
and HR-driven, so that scope is always accurate without manual maintenance.

## Why AU Membership Rules Change the Equation

In the flat-delegation model without OrgPath, AU membership is managed
manually. A user moves from Finance to Legal, and someone must remove them
from `AU-Department-Finance` and add them to `AU-Department-Legal`. Until
that happens, the departing-Finance employee can still have their password
reset by the Finance helpdesk, and the Legal helpdesk cannot yet assist
them. Scope is only as accurate as the most recent manual update.

With OrgPath, AU membership is driven by facet predicates evaluated
continuously against each user's `extensionAttribute` values:

```text
AU-Department-Finance
  membership rule: (attr2 -eq "Finance")

AU-Department-Legal
  membership rule: (attr2 -eq "Legal")
```

When HR updates the user's department record, the provisioning pipeline
writes the new value to `extensionAttribute2`. Both AU membership rules
re-evaluate. The user leaves Finance's AU and enters Legal's AU
automatically. No manual intervention. No window of incorrect scope.

The role assignments bound to each AU do not change. The scope they express
stays accurate because the membership that defines the scope is governed by
the same SSOT that governs the org chart.

This is the mechanism that makes AU-based delegation structurally equivalent
to OU-based delegation — not inheritance, but deterministic, attribute-driven
membership that tracks organizational position.

## The Three-Tier Delegation Model

The canonical delegation model (UIAO_154) organizes AUs into three tiers
that mirror the organizational hierarchy without requiring inheritance
between them:

| Tier | AU Pattern | Membership Rule | Typical Roles |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 — Enterprise | `AU-Enterprise` | `(attr2 -ne "")` — any governed user | Global Reader, Security Reader |
| Tier 2 — Department | `AU-Department-[DEPT]` | `(attr2 -eq "[DEPT]")` | User Administrator, Groups Administrator |
| Tier 3 — Division | `AU-[DEPT]-[DIV]` | `(attr2 -eq "[DEPT]") and (attr3 -eq "[DIV]")` | Helpdesk Administrator, Password Administrator |
| Cross-cutting | `AU-[FACETS]-[VALUE]` | Multi-facet predicate | Authentication Administrator |

Each tier is independent — there is no AU-to-AU inheritance — but scope
at each tier is always accurate because OrgPath facets define it. A
Helpdesk Administrator scoped to `AU-IT-InfraOps` can only act on users
whose `extensionAttribute2` is `IT` and `extensionAttribute3` is
`InfraOps`. When a user's division changes, they leave the AU on the next
membership evaluation; the helpdesk technician's scope adjusts without any
change to the role assignment.

## AD Delegation Patterns — Entra ID Equivalents

Every common Active Directory delegation pattern has a direct Entra
equivalent built from AU + OrgPath facet predicate + scoped role. The
table below covers the patterns administrators encounter in practice:

| Active Directory pattern | Entra ID equivalent |
|---|---|
| Helpdesk resets passwords on `OU=Baltimore` | Authentication Administrator scoped to `AU-Baltimore` (rule: `attr5 -eq "CC-BAL"`) |
| IT staff manages users in `OU=East-Region` | User Administrator scoped to `AU-US-East` (rule: `attr1 -eq "EASTUS"`) |
| Department admin creates groups on `OU=Finance` | Groups Administrator scoped to `AU-Department-Finance` |
| Read-only view of all users for audit | Global Reader at tenant scope — no AU needed |
| GPO controls Intune enrollment for a specific OU | Intune policy set targeted at the equivalent OrgPath dynamic group |
| Site-linked GPO enforces network-based policy | Conditional Access named location + compliance policy, targeted by OrgPath group |
| Service account management on `OU=ServiceAccounts` | Workload Identity Administrator (PIM-gated), scoped to service-account AU |
| Domain Admin — forest-level privilege | Global Administrator, PIM-eligible only — never permanently active |
| Schema Admin, Enterprise Admin | Privileged Role Administrator via PIM; requires dual approval |
| Fine-grained password policy applied to specific OU | Entra ID authentication policy targeted at OrgPath dynamic group |

::: {.callout-important}
**Never substitute tenant-wide role assignments for AU-scoped ones.**
If a role can be AU-scoped, it must be AU-scoped. Unscoped assignments
for roles that have an AU-scope equivalent are a governance finding under
UIAO_154 Governance Rule 4.
:::

## PIM: The Activation Layer

Administrative Units define who can manage what objects. PIM defines
whether that authority is available continuously or only on explicit,
approved, time-bounded elevation. In the UIAO governance model, these
two mechanisms are always used together:

* Role assignments to AUs are **eligible**, not active. A technician
  who is a member of `AU-IT-InfraOps` with Helpdesk Administrator eligible
  cannot act until they activate via PIM.
* Activation requires written justification and, for elevated roles,
  supervisor approval and FIDO2 MFA.
* Activation is time-bounded. A 4-hour helpdesk window is the standard
  maximum. The session ends; the role is no longer active.
* Every activation generates an immutable audit event in Entra ID Audit
  Logs, tied to the ServiceNow RITM that authorized the work.

The combination of AU scoping and PIM gating produces the closest
available analog to the AD model of OU-scoped ACLs with delegated control
— with the addition of time-bounding and audit that AD delegation natively
lacked.

## Multi-Facet AUs: Cross-Cutting Scope

Some delegation requirements cut across the standard department/division
hierarchy. A privileged-access team that must manage high-clearance users
regardless of department. A security team with authentication rights over
all contractor accounts. These scenarios are handled with cross-cutting
AUs whose membership rules compose facets from multiple dimensions:

```text
AU-Region-EASTUS-Privileged
  membership rule:
    (attr1 -eq "EASTUS") and (attr8 -eq "SECRET")
  roles:
    Authentication Administrator (scoped to this AU)

AU-Classification-Contractor-All
  membership rule:
    (attr6 -eq "Contractor")
  roles:
    Helpdesk Administrator (scoped to this AU)
    Password Administrator (scoped to this AU)

AU-IT-InfraOps-FullTime
  membership rule:
    (attr2 -eq "IT") and (attr3 -eq "InfraOps") and (attr6 -eq "Employee")
  roles:
    Groups Administrator (scoped to this AU)
```

The membership rules are still facet predicates — the same OrgPath SSOT
governs them. Cross-cutting AUs compose predicates with boolean operators
rather than traversing an OU path. There is no inheritance problem to solve
because the rule itself expresses exactly the scope needed.

## What This Replaces, and What It Does Not

The AU + OrgPath model reproduces the functional outcomes of OU-based
delegation with explicit, auditable construction rather than structural
inheritance. What it provides:

* Scoped management authority that tracks organizational position without
  manual maintenance
* Audit-grade evidence of every role activation (PIM logs), with the
  organizational scope of the action captured in the AU record
* Governance Rule 4 enforcement that prevents scope creep through
  unscoped role assignments
* Dynamic adjustment when org structure changes — membership rules
  re-evaluate continuously

What it does not reproduce from Active Directory:

* **Inherited scope.** Roles do not flow from a parent AU to child AUs.
  Each tier's roles must be assigned independently. This is explicit
  work — but explicit work that is auditable, not implicit work that
  silently accumulates.
* **Automatic scope extension.** Adding a new division does not
  automatically create a Tier 3 AU and assign helpdesk access to it.
  The AU must be defined, the membership rule authored, and the role
  assigned. The OrgPath codebook change triggers this obligation; it does
  not execute it.

Both gaps are operational, not architectural. They are addressed by the
AU provisioning workflow (ADR-037) and the delegation matrix (UIAO_154),
which together make AU lifecycle a governed, pipeline-driven process rather
than a manual one.
